raw_case_text:
A 79-year-old man with hypertension and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) presented with dysphasia after the first cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody). He was initially diagnosed with CLL a year earlier and initiated therapy due to fatigue and progressive anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL) without prior infections. His baseline absolute neutrophil count was 2.7 x 109/L, absolute lymphocyte count was 16.3 x 109/L, absolute monocyte count was 0.3 x 109/L, and IgG level obtained at diagnosis was 805 mg/dL. There was no history of use of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive medications. He used to work in construction but had retired many years prior and had remained very active in his garden until initiation of chemotherapy. There was no other pertinent medical, surgical, social, or family history. Except for slurred speech, his physical exam was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed 3 distinct left temporal and parietal lobe abscesses with significant edema (Figure 1), for which he was started on high-dose dexamethasone 4 mg four times daily. Chest CT revealed a pulmonary nodule (Figure 2). Blood cultures, serum cryptococcal Ag, Aspergillus Ag (galactomannan, using the Platelia Aspergillus enzyme immunoassay (EIA)), and beta-D-glucan (betaDg) were negative. Stereotactic brain biopsy of one of the abscesses failed to include its necrotic core and was nondiagnostic. Plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing (cfDNA NGS) showed a strong signal for Nocardia abscessus. Therefore, the patient was discharged on dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily, ceftriaxone, minocycline, and linezolid, which was subsequently discontinued because of thrombocytopenia.
Repeat imaging revealed decrease in the size of the brain abscesses (Figure 1) and of the pulmonary nodule with central cavitation (Figure 2). However, he had recurrence of dysphasia and brain edema on imaging soon after tapering and discontinuation of dexamethasone approximately 6 weeks from initial presentation. He was restarted on dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily, with a plan for a slower taper.
After two more weeks, approximately two months from his initial presentation, he was admitted to the intensive care unit with multiorgan (respiratory, renal, and heart) failure. Brain MRI showed significant decrease in the size of previous abscesses, but also many new infarcts (Figure 1). Chest CT showed multiple lung masses with cavitation, consistent with new abscesses (Figure 3). Repeat betaDg was negative, but galactomannan was >9.3 (EIA assay cut-off). His family opted for comfort measures only, and kindly agreed to an autopsy.
Autopsy showed (1) acute IMI involving both lungs. Hyphal morphology was consistent with Aspergillus species (septate, narrow-angled, Figure 4). Lung cultures were positive for Aspergillus fumigatus. (2) Acute IMI in both heart ventricles, with wide-angled, aseptate hyphae, consistent with mucormycosis (Figure 5); molecular studies (28 s/internal transcriber sequence (ITS) RNA identification, University of Washington, Seattle) came back positive for Lichtheimia corymbifera. (3) Cervical, mediastinal lymph node, thyroid gland, and left kidney (Figure 5) IMI. (4) Cerebral abscesses of the left temporal and parietal lobes with fungal organisms in the blood vessels and brain parenchyma, consistent with mucorales (Figure 6), and filamentous organisms identified with GMS/FITE stains, consistent with Nocardia (Figure 7).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 79-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with acute dysphasia after his first cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Shortly after completing his first cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), the patient presented with slurred speech/dysphasia. Six weeks later, upon tapering dexamethasone, his dysphasia and cerebral edema recurred, and at 2 months from initial presentation he was admitted to the ICU with multiorgan (respiratory, renal, and cardiac) failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) diagnosed 1 year prior (baseline ANC 2.7 x 10^9/L, ALC 16.3 x 10^9/L, AMC 0.3 x 10^9/L, Hb 8.9 g/dL, IgG 805 mg/dL) recently started on chlorambucil and obinutuzumab; hypertension; retired construction worker and avid gardener until chemotherapy initiation; no prior corticosteroid use.

objective.physical_examination: Slurred speech/dysphasia with an otherwise unremarkable initial physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood cultures, serum cryptococcal antigen, serum Aspergillus galactomannan (Platelia EIA), and serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan were all negative. At ICU admission 2 months later, repeat serum beta-D-glucan remained negative while serum Aspergillus galactomannan was strongly positive at >9.3 (EIA index).
objective.advanced_workup: Initial brain MRI revealed three distinct abscesses in the left temporal and parietal lobes with marked vasogenic edema; chest CT showed a solitary pulmonary nodule. Stereotactic brain biopsy missed the necrotic core and was nondiagnostic, whereas plasma microbial cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing (cfDNA NGS) detected a strong signal for Nocardia abscessus. Follow-up imaging at 6-8 weeks showed shrinkage of the initial brain abscesses and central cavitation of the lung nodule, followed at 2 months by multiple new cerebral infarcts on brain MRI and multiple new cavitating lung masses on chest CT.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cerebral nocardiosis caused by Nocardia abscessus complicated by fatal disseminated co-infection with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) and angioinvasive mucormycosis (Lichtheimia corymbifera involving the brain, myocardium, thyroid, lymph nodes, and left kidney) following prolonged high-dose dexamethasone was confirmed via plasma cfDNA NGS and post-mortem autopsy (which demonstrated GMS/Fite-positive Nocardia filaments alongside Mucorales hyphae in the left temporoparietal brain abscesses, 28S/ITS-confirmed Lichtheimia corymbifera in biventricular cardiac/multiorgan lesions, and culture-confirmed Aspergillus fumigatus in both lungs). Initial treatment with dexamethasone (4 mg QID, tapered and restarted at 4 mg BID), ceftriaxone, minocycline, and linezolid (stopped for thrombocytopenia) had reduced the nocardial abscesses, but the patient died in the ICU at 2 months from disseminated invasive mold superinfection and multiorgan failure.
